# Method for the Continuous Production of Metal-Plastic Composite Webs

### Overview
The present invention relates to a method for producing high-performance metal-plastic composite webs. The resulting material features a sandwich-style arrangement comprising a central plastic core layer that is integrally bonded between an upper and a lower outer metal cover layer, offering a lightweight yet structurally rigid material solution.

### Process Description

#### Stage 1: Metal Pretreatment and Storage
The manufacturing process begins by surface-treating the metal components to ensure maximum bond strength. Upper and lower continuous metal strips are fed into a dedicated, standalone pretreatment line. Within this line, both metal strips receive a uniform coating of a specialized adhesion promoter across their bonding surfaces. Immediately following the application and curing of the adhesion promoter, the pretreated metal strips are wound up into coils. Decoupling the surface preparation step into a dedicated line allows for optimized coating parameters and flexible intermediate storage of the pretreated metal coils.

#### Stage 2: Lamination and Composite Formation
In a subsequent step, the pretreated metal coils and a continuous plastic core web are transferred to a laminating line that operates independently of the pretreatment line. Within the laminating line, the pretreated upper and lower metal strips are unwound and aligned on opposite sides of the plastic core web. 

The final composite web is then continuously formed as the combined layers pass through the laminating line. By applying a controlled combination of heat and pressure, the adhesion promoter is activated, fusing the outer metal layers permanently to the central plastic web. 

### Conclusion
This decoupled, continuous production method ensures optimal surface activation and bonding, yielding a high-quality metal-plastic composite web characterized by superior delamination resistance and structural integrity.

# Advanced Manufacturing Method for Metal-Plastic-Metal Sandwich Composite Sheets

## 1. Introduction
Metal-plastic-metal composite sheets—frequently featuring an inner core of a lightweight thermoplastic material sandwiched between two thin metallic face sheets—have become vital structural materials across the architectural, automotive, and transportation industries. They offer an exceptional strength-to-weight ratio, vibration damping, and excellent formability. 

To manufacture these materials at an industrial scale, a two-stage, decoupled process has been developed. By separating the initial metal surface pretreatment from the final thermal consolidation stage, manufacturers achieve maximum process flexibility, higher production speeds, and superior bond integrity across the final composite web.

---

## 2. Phase 1: Pretreatment and Coating Line
The process begins with raw metal strips (typically aluminum, steel, or stainless steel) supplied in large coils. The primary goal of this initial phase is to prepare the metal surfaces for long-term interfacial adhesion before introducing the core material.

1. **Uncoiling and Surface Preparation:** 
   The continuous metal strips are uncoiled and passed through a multi-stage cleaning zone. Here, oils, oxides, and contaminants are chemically removed via alkaline degreasing, rinsing, and mechanical brushing to maximize surface energy.

2. **Application of Adhesion Promoter:**
   Once cleaned and dried, the interior-facing sides of the metal strips enter a coil-coating unit. A high-performance adhesion promoter—typically a liquid polymer primer, modified polyolefin adhesive, or silane-based coupling agent—is applied continuously and evenly across the moving metal web using reverse roll-coaters.

3. **Curing and Recoiling:**
   The coated strips pass through a drying oven where the adhesion promoter is thermally cured or partially cross-linked. The pretreated metal strips are then cooled and wound back into tight coils. 

Because this pretreatment phase operates independently of the downstream laminating line, it can run at high line speeds, ensuring optimal efficiency and uniform coating quality.

---

## 3. Phase 2: Decoupled Laminating and Consolidation Line
In the second stage of production, the pretreated metal coils are transferred to a dedicated laminating line where they are permanently joined with a plastic core web.

```
[Top Metal Coil] ---------\
                           \
[Plastic Web / Extruder] ---> [ Heating & Pressure Zone ] ---> [ Cooling Zone ] ---> [ Cutting & Stacking ]
                           /  (Integrally Bonded Sheet)
[Bottom Metal Coil] ------/
```

1. **Material Feed:**
   Two rolls of the pretreated metal strip are mounted onto uncoilers at the head of the laminating line—one forming the upper surface layer, the other forming the lower layer. Simultaneously, a continuous plastic web (such as polyethylene, polypropylene, or a mineral-filled fire-retardant thermoplastic resin) is fed into the center. This plastic core can either be unwound from a prefabricated roll or extruded directly inline between the two metal sheets.

2. **Thermal Activation and Pressing:**
   The three layers—top metal, plastic core, and bottom metal—are merged as they enter a continuous laminating unit, such as a double-belt press or a system of heated calendaring rolls. Controlled heat is applied to activate the pre-applied adhesion promoter and soften the outer boundaries of the plastic core. Concurrently, precise mechanical pressure is exerted to press the metal skins firmly into the molten surface of the core.

3. **Integral Bonding and Cooling:**
   Under sustained heat and pressure, the adhesion promoter creates a continuous, high-strength chemical and mechanical bond across the entire width of the composite web. The consolidated sandwich web then passes into a controlled cooling zone, solidifying the thermoplastic core and locking in the structural integrity of the sheet without inducing internal stress or warping.

4. **Sizing and Finishing:**
   Once cooled, the continuously produced composite web is cut to desired lengths by a flying shear or cross-cut saw, yielding flat, ready-to-use composite panels.

---

## 4. Key Advantages of the Decoupled Process

* **Operational Efficiency:** Coil coating lines typically run much faster than laminating lines. Decoupling the two operations prevents the slower laminating stage from creating a bottleneck on the coating line.
* **Production Flexibility:** Pretreated metal coils can be manufactured in large batches and stored in inventory. They can later be laminated with different core thicknesses, plastic densities, or core compositions based on customer demand, without needing to restart the chemical coating process.
* **Superior Quality Control:** Separating the chemical surface treatment from the thermal joining phase allows for independent quality checks of the metal coating prior to final assembly, significantly reducing material scrap and ensuring consistent delamination resistance.

Three letters. Two consonants and a single vowel. It slips off the tongue almost unnoticed, yet it dominates the English language. It is "the"—the most frequently used word in our vocabulary, an unsung giant hiding in plain sight.

Grammatically, it is classified as a definite article, but conceptually, it is an architect of focus. Consider the profound shift that occurs when it enters a sentence. There is a vast, existential difference between asking for "a key" and asking for "*the* key." "A key" belongs to an infinite pool of possibilities; it is generic, replaceable, and vague. But "*the* key" demands immediate attention. It points an invisible finger, plucking one singular object out of the chaotic background of the universe and declaring: *this one matters.*

Because of this power to specify, "the" carries immense psychological and cultural weight. We use it to bestow grandeur, authority, and finality. A leader is not just *a* president, but *The* President. A musician might dream of playing not just *a* stage, but *The* Stage. When a journey closes, it does not simply stop—it arrives at *The End*. By attaching these three letters to a noun, we elevate the ordinary into the absolute. 

Yet, for all its structural majesty, "the" remains remarkably humble. It is the invisible glue of thought, spoken thousands of times a day without a second glance. It bridges the gap between speaker and listener, silently establishing a shared context. It assumes that we are looking at the same horizon, reading the same page, and living in the same moment.

In a world filled with noisy, expressive, multi-syllable words, "the" quietly does the heavy lifting of human communication. It is a paradox of language: the smallest word with the largest reach, forever transforming the vast and indefinite into something real, tangible, and known.

---

# PATENT SPECIFICATION

**TITLE OF THE INVENTION:**
CONTINUOUS METHOD FOR MANUFACTURING METAL-POLYMER-METAL LAMINATES UTILIZING DECOUPLED ADHESIVE COIL PREPARATION AND THERMAL-PRESSURE LAMINATION

---

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION
[0001] The present invention relates generally to continuous manufacturing methods for composite material sheets. More particularly, the invention relates to a continuous method for fabricating three-layer sandwich sheets comprising an upper metal skin, a central polymeric core, and a lower metal skin, wherein the chemical pre-treatment and adhesive coating of the metal coils are performed on an independent process line spatially and operationally decoupled from the continuous lamination line.

---

## BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION
[0002] Lightweight structural materials, such as Metal-Polymer-Metal (MPM) sandwich panels, are increasingly utilized in the automotive, aerospace, building construction, and consumer electronics industries. These laminates typically consist of a low-density thermoplastic core (e.g., polyethylene, polypropylene, or polyamide) bonded between two thin high-strength metal skins (e.g., aluminum, steel, or stainless steel).

[0003] Conventional continuous production of MPM sheets typically employs an fully integrated inline process. In such inline processes, raw metal coils are continuously unwound, cleaned, chemically etched, coated with liquid primer or adhesive, dried in inline ovens, immediately mated with a polymer core (either via direct melt extrusion or pre-formed film), passing through a lamination nip, and cooled. 

[0004] Integrated inline processes present significant operational and economic drawbacks:
1. **Speed Mismatch:** High-speed coil coating lines typically operate optimally at linear speeds of 50 to 150 meters per minute. Conversely, heavy thermal-pressure lamination and extrusion processes run significantly slower, typically 5 to 25 meters per minute due to heat transfer limits in the thick polymer core. Combining them forces the coating line to run at suboptimal, low speeds, leading to degraded coating quality and energy inefficiency in large drying ovens.
2. **Capital and Spatial Footprint:** Integrated lines require immense physical plant space to accommodate cleaning baths, drying ovens, extruders, double-belt presses, and cooling zones sequentially.
3. **Operational Downtime:** Any interruption in the lamination section (e.g., polymer die blockage, sheet jam) requires stopping the entire chemical application line, leading to substantial raw material scrap and thermal degradation of stagnant metal strips inside inline ovens.

[0005] Therefore, there exists a need for an improved continuous manufacturing process that decouples the surface preparation and adhesive coating steps from the thermal lamination process, allowing each stage to operate at its respective optimal process parameters.

---

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION
[0006] The present invention addresses the aforementioned deficiencies by providing a method for manufacturing a continuous three-layer metal-polymer-metal sandwich sheet using two decoupled, independent manufacturing lines: a **Coil Pre-Treatment Line (Line A)** and a **Continuous Lamination Line (Line B)**.

[0007] In a primary embodiment of the invention, the method comprises:
1. **Line A (Decoupled Pre-Treatment):**
   - Continuously unwinding a raw metal coil;
   - Pre-treating at least one major surface of the metal strip (cleaning/conversion coating);
   - Applying a heat-activatable, non-tacky adhesive system to the treated surface;
   - Thermally curing or drying the adhesive to a non-tacky, stable "B-stage" state; and
   - Rewinding the pre-treated, adhesive-coated metal strip into a intermediate coated coil.

2. **Intermediary Storage/Transport:**
   - Storing or transporting the intermediate coated coils at ambient temperature, where the adhesive remains non-blocking and shelf-stable for an extended period.

3. **Line B (Decoupled Continuous Lamination):**
   - Unwinding a first pre-coated metal coil (top skin) and a second pre-coated metal coil (bottom skin) on a continuous lamination line spatially isolated from Line A;
   - Continuously feeding a molten or pre-formed solid thermoplastic core material between the adhesive-coated surfaces of the first and second metal skins;
   - Heating the assembly to activate the pre-applied adhesive and soften the interface of the polymeric core;
   - Consolidating the three layers under continuous pressure in a lamination zone;
   - Cooling the consolidated sandwich sheet; and
   - Cutting the continuous sheet into discrete panels.

---

## BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS
[0008] **FIG. 1** is a schematic flow diagram illustrating the first processing line (Line A) for pre-treating and applying adhesive to metal coils.
[0009] **FIG. 2** is a schematic flow diagram illustrating the second processing line (Line B) for continuous thermal-pressure lamination using the pre-coated coils produced by Line A.

---

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF PREFERRED EMBODIMENTS

### 1. Line A: Decoupled Coil Coating Process
[0010] Referring to **FIG. 1**, a metal substrate [10] (e.g., aluminum alloy 5052 or galvanized steel, thickness 0.15 mm to 0.8 mm) is unwound from an uncoiler [12] at a first line speed ($V_1$), preferably between 40 m/min and 120 m/min.

[0011] The metal strip passes through a pre-treatment section [14] comprising degreasing, acid/alkaline washing, and chemical conversion coating (e.g., silane, titanate, or zirconium-based pre-treatments) to maximize metal-to-polymer corrosion resistance and bonding strength.

[0012] The pre-treated strip enters a coating station [16], preferably a reverse roll coater or slot-die coater, where a liquid, heat-activatable adhesive layer [18] is applied to at least one surface. The adhesive is preferably selected from maleic anhydride modified polyolefins, epoxy-amine dispersions, or polyurethane-based hot-melt precursors. The dry coat weight is targeted between 3 $\text{g/m}^2$ and 25 $\text{g/m}^2$.

[0013] The wet strip passes through a curing/drying oven [20] maintained at temperatures sufficient to evaporate solvents/water and partially react the adhesive to a non-tacky "B-stage" state (e.g., Peak Metal Temperature of 180°C to 240°C). Crucially, the adhesive must dry to a state where it does not exhibit tackiness at room temperature.

[0014] After forced air cooling [22], the coated metal strip is rewound onto a recoiler [24] to form a stable **Adhesive Pre-Coated Metal Coil [26]**. These coils [26] are stored at ambient temperatures without blocking (adhering to adjacent layer wraps) for periods ranging from hours to months.

---

### 2. Line B: Decoupled Continuous Lamination Process
[0015] Referring to **FIG. 2**, the continuous lamination process takes place on Line B, which is entirely physically decoupled from Line A, operating independently at a second line speed ($V_2$), where $V_2 < V_1$ (preferably $V_2$ is between 2 m/min and 20 m/min).

[0016] Two pre-coated coils [26a, 26b] prepared on Line A are mounted on a upper uncoiler [30a] and lower uncoiler [30b], respectively. The coils are unwound such that their adhesive-coated faces [18a, 18b] face inward toward each other.

[0017] A central thermoplastic polymer core [32] (e.g., polypropylene, high-density polyethylene, or polyamide, thickness 0.5 mm to 4.0 mm) is continuously introduced between the two metal skins. In one embodiment, the core [32] is directly extruded from a wide-slot sheet die connected to a single- or twin-screw extruder [34]. In an alternative embodiment, the core [32] is unwound from a solid pre-extruded roll.

[0018] The pre-assembly (top skin [26a], core [32], bottom skin [26b]) enters a pre-heating zone [36] utilizing Infrared (IR) heaters, induction heating coils, or hot air circulation. The pre-heating activates the B-staged adhesive layers [18a, 18b] to a molten, tacky state and pre-heats the surfaces of the polymer core [32].

[0019] The activated pre-assembly passes into a continuous lamination zone [38], preferably a continuous double-belt press or a series of heated nip rollers. Heat ($T_{lam} = 140^\circ\text{C}$ to $260^\circ\text{C}$) and continuous pressure ($P_{lam} = 0.1\text{ MPa}$ to $3.0\text{ MPa}$) are simultaneously applied. This pressure forces the reactivated adhesive to wet out the interfaces between the metal skins and the core, forming strong chemical bonds and mechanical interlocking.

[0020] The consolidated continuous 3-layer sandwich sheet moves through a cooling section [40] (water-cooled platen belts or air knives) under maintained pressure to solidify the thermoplastic core and set the adhesive bonds, preventing delamination due to thermal stress mismatch.

[0021] The cooled sandwich sheet [42] is continuously measured by optical sensors and cut into discrete lengths using a flying shear or travelling saw unit [44].

---

## WE CLAIM (CLAIMS)

1. A continuous method for manufacturing a three-layer metal-polymer-metal sandwich sheet, the method comprising:
   - **(a)** on a first processing line operating at a first line speed:
     - unwinding a continuous metal strip from a raw coil;
     - applying a chemical pre-treatment to at least one major surface of the metal strip;
     - applying a layer of a heat-activatable adhesive to the pre-treated surface;
     - drying or partially curing the adhesive layer to form a dry-to-touch, non-tacky adhesive coating; and
     - rewinding the pre-treated, adhesive-coated metal strip into an intermediate pre-coated coil;
   - **(b)** transferring at least a first intermediate pre-coated coil and a second intermediate pre-coated coil to a second processing line physically decoupled and operationally independent from the first processing line; and
   - **(c)** on the second processing line operating at a second line speed:
     - continuously unwinding the first intermediate pre-coated coil as a top skin and the second intermediate pre-coated coil as a bottom skin such that their respective adhesive coatings face inward;
     - continuously introducing a polymeric core material between the inward-facing adhesive coatings of the top and bottom skins;
     - applying heat to activate the pre-applied adhesive coatings;
     - continuously applying pressure to laminate the top skin, polymeric core material, and bottom skin into a unified three-layer

**characterized in that** 

the step of applying the adhesion promoter composition is executed on a dedicated pretreatment line ($V$), and the step of laminating the metallic substrate with the polymer core or film is executed on a separate laminating line ($L$), wherein said pretreatment line ($V$) and said laminating line ($L$) are operationally and spatially decoupled from one another.

In a preferred embodiment of the invention, the method comprises the sequential steps of:
1. Subjecting a metallic strip to a surface cleaning and conversion treatment on the pretreatment line ($V$);
2. Applying an liquid or liquid-dispersed adhesion promoter coating to at least one surface of the moving metallic strip on said pretreatment line ($V$);
3. Curing or drying said adhesion promoter coating on the pretreatment line ($V$) to yield a pre-coated metallic intermediate;
4. Temporarily storing or coiling said pre-coated metallic intermediate;
5. Transferring said pre-coated metallic intermediate to the laminating line ($L$); and
6. Feeding the pre-coated metallic intermediate and a polymeric substrate into the laminating line ($L$) to bond the pre-coated metallic intermediate to the polymeric substrate under predefined thermal and mechanical conditions.

Advantageously, the operational decoupling of the pretreatment line ($V$) and the laminating line ($L$) allows the line speed ($v_V$) of the pretreatment line ($V$) to be controlled and varied independently of the line speed ($v_L$) of the laminating line ($L$). 

Furthermore, this operational decoupling eliminates the thermal inertia feedback between the curing of the adhesion promoter and the downstream lamination process, thereby optimizing energy consumption, preventing thermal degradation of the adhesion promoter, and maximizing throughput on both respective processing lines.

* **"Spatially and Operationally Decoupled":** This phrase is key. It ensures you capture both physical separation (different machines/rooms) and temporal separation (doing step 1 today, storing it, and doing step 2 next week).
